name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q01 - Position of hydrogen and commercial dihydrogen production

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding hydrogen and the commercial production of dihydrogen:

I. Hydrogen resembles alkali metals in having a \(1s^1\) outer electronic configuration and halogens in being one electron short of the nearest noble gas configuration.

II. The \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion formed by loss of an electron from a hydrogen atom has a size of about \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ pm}\) and exists freely in aqueous solutions.

III. High-purity (\(>99.95\%\)) dihydrogen is obtained commercially by electrolysing warm aqueous barium hydroxide solution between nickel electrodes.

IV. The mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) obtained by reacting steam with hydrocarbons or coke at \(1270\text{ K}\) is called water gas or synthesis gas (syngas).

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Position of Hydrogen in the Periodic Table
Hydrogen has the electronic configuration \(1s^1\). It resembles alkali metals (\(ns^1\)) by losing one electron to form \(\mathrm{H}^+\) and forming oxides, halides, and sulphides. At the same time, it is one electron short of the helium configuration (\(1s^2\)), resembling halogens (\(ns^2np^5\)) in forming diatomic molecules and covalent compounds. Therefore, the claim regarding hydrogen's dual resemblance to alkali metals and halogens is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Size and Existence of the \(\mathrm{H}^+\) Ion
Loss of the single electron from a hydrogen atom leaves behind a bare proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) with a nuclear size of \(\sim 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ pm}\), which is extremely small compared to normal atomic and ionic sizes of \(50\text{ to }200\text{ pm}\). Due to this extremely high charge density, \(\mathrm{H}^+\) never exists freely and is always associated with other atoms or molecules (for instance, as \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) in water). Hence, the claim that \(\mathrm{H}^+\) exists freely in aqueous solutions is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation — Commercial Electrolytic Production of Dihydrogen
Electrolysis of warm aqueous barium hydroxide solution between nickel electrodes yields high-purity (\(>99.95\%\)) dihydrogen. Hence, the claim regarding high-purity dihydrogen production is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation — Water Gas / Syngas Formation
When steam reacts with hydrocarbons or coke at \(1270\text{ K}\) (in the presence of a nickel catalyst for hydrocarbons), a mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) is formed:
\[\mathrm{C}(\text{s}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\text{g}) \xrightarrow{1270\text{ K}} \mathrm{CO}(\text{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2(\text{g})\]
This mixture of \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) is known as water gas, and because it is used in the synthesis of methanol and hydrocarbons, it is also called synthesis gas or syngas. Hence, this claim is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding hydrogen's resemblance to alkali metals and halogens, the electrolytic preparation of high-purity dihydrogen using barium hydroxide and nickel electrodes, and the formation of water gas (syngas) at \(1270\text{ K}\) are correct, whereas the claim that \(\mathrm{H}^+\) exists freely is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q02 - Structure, properties, and hydrates of water

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements about water and its crystalline form, ice:

I. In the gas phase, water is a bent molecule with an \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\) bond angle of \(104.5^{\circ}\) and an \(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\) bond length of \(95.7\text{ pm}\).

II. In the crystal structure of ice, each oxygen atom is surrounded tetrahedrally by four other oxygen atoms at a distance of \(276\text{ pm}\).

III. Water is amphoteric in nature, acting as a Brønsted base towards \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and as a Brønsted acid towards \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\).

IV. In \(\mathrm{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), four water molecules are coordinated to \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) and only one water molecule is hydrogen-bonded outside the coordination sphere.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Structure of Water in the Gas Phase
In the gas phase, an isolated water molecule has a bent geometry due to two lone pairs on the oxygen atom, giving an \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\) bond angle of \(104.5^{\circ}\) and an \(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\) bond length of \(95.7\text{ pm}\). Thus, the claim regarding the gas-phase geometry of water is correct.

Step 2: Conceptual Principle — Crystal Structure of Ice
X-ray examination of ice crystals reveals a highly ordered three-dimensional hydrogen-bonded network in which each oxygen atom is surrounded tetrahedrally by four other oxygen atoms at a distance of \(276\text{ pm}\). Thus, the claim regarding the tetrahedral arrangement in ice is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation — Amphoteric Behaviour of Water
In the Brønsted–Lowry sense, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Water donates a proton to \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) (acting as a Brønsted acid) and accepts a proton from \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) (acting as a Brønsted base):
\[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\text{l}) + \mathrm{NH}_3(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{OH}^-(\text{aq}) + \mathrm{NH}_4^+(\text{aq})\]
\[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\text{l}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+(\text{aq}) + \mathrm{HS}^-(\text{aq})\]
Therefore, the claim that water acts as a Brønsted base towards \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and as a Brønsted acid towards \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) reverses the roles and is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation — Hydrate Bonding in \(\mathrm{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
Blue vitriol is formulated as \([\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_4]^{2+}\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-} \cdot \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\). Inside the coordination sphere, four water molecules are coordinated to the \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ion, while the fifth water molecule lies outside the coordination sphere and is hydrogen-bonded. Thus, the claim regarding the distribution of water molecules in \(\mathrm{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims describing the gas-phase bond angle and bond length of water, the tetrahedral oxygen arrangement in ice, and the single hydrogen-bonded water molecule in \(\mathrm{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) are correct, while the claim reversing water's Brønsted acid-base roles with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROGEN_MCQ_Q03 - Syngas shift reaction, peroxide redox, heavy water, and fuel energy

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements:

I. In the water-gas shift reaction, \(\mathrm{CO}\) of syngas reacts with steam at \(673\text{ K}\) in the presence of an iron chromate catalyst to yield \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\), and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) is removed by scrubbing with sodium arsenite solution.

II. Hydrogen peroxide oxidises \(\mathrm{PbS}\) to \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4\) in acidic medium and reduces \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) to \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\) in basic medium.

III. Heavy water (\(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\)) has a higher melting point (\(276.8\text{ K}\)) and a higher temperature of maximum density (\(284.2\text{ K}\)) than ordinary water (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)).

IV. On a mass-for-mass basis, liquid octane releases nearly three times as much energy on combustion as gaseous dihydrogen.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We are evaluating four quantitative and reaction-based claims: (a) the water-gas shift reaction conditions and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) scrubbing reagent, (b) redox reactions of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) with \(\mathrm{PbS}\) and \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\), (c) physical constants of \(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\) versus \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (\(T_{\text{m}}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}) = 273.0\text{ K}\), \(T_{\text{max density}}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}) = 276.98\text{ K}\)), and (d) combustion energy per gram of gaseous \(\mathrm{H}_2\) (\(143\text{ kJ g}^{-1}\)) versus liquid octane (\(47\text{ kJ g}^{-1}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All physical constants and combustion enthalpies are taken at the standard reference conditions reported for the respective species, and redox behaviour is evaluated by oxidation-state changes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Water-gas shift reaction:
\[\mathrm{CO}(\text{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\text{g}) \xrightarrow[\text{iron chromate}]{673\text{ K}} \mathrm{CO}_2(\text{g}) + \mathrm{H}_2(\text{g})\]
2. Redox reactions of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\):
\[\mathrm{PbS}(\text{s}) + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{PbSO}_4(\text{s}) + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\text{l})\]
\[2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 3\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 2\mathrm{OH}^-\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, in the water-gas shift reaction, \(\mathrm{CO}\) reacts with steam at \(673\text{ K}\) over an iron chromate catalyst to increase \(\mathrm{H}_2\) yield, and the \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) formed is removed by scrubbing with sodium arsenite solution. Thus, this claim is correct.

Second, in acidic medium, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) oxidises \(\mathrm{S}^{2-}\) in \(\mathrm{PbS}\) (\(-2\) oxidation state) to \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\) in \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4\) (\(+6\) oxidation state). In basic medium, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) reduces \(\mathrm{Mn}\) in \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) (\(+7\) oxidation state) to \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\) (\(+4\) oxidation state). Thus, this redox claim is correct.

Third, comparing physical properties, \(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\) melts at \(276.8\text{ K}\) (versus \(273.0\text{ K}\) for \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) and reaches maximum density at \(284.2\text{ K}\) (versus \(276.98\text{ K}\) for \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)). Both values for \(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\) are higher than for \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), so this claim is correct.

Fourth, comparing energy released per gram on combustion, gaseous dihydrogen releases \(143\text{ kJ g}^{-1}\) whereas liquid octane releases \(47\text{ kJ g}^{-1}\). The ratio is:
\[\frac{143\text{ kJ g}^{-1}}{47\text{ kJ g}^{-1}} \approx 3.04\]
This shows that dihydrogen releases nearly three times as much energy per gram as octane, not the reverse. Thus, the claim that liquid octane releases nearly three times as much energy per gram as gaseous dihydrogen is incorrect.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All units, temperatures, oxidation states, and energy-per-gram ratios are verified. The claims regarding the water-gas shift reaction, the redox reactions of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\), and the higher melting point and maximum-density temperature of \(\mathrm{D}_2\mathrm{O}\) are correct, while the claim regarding the mass-basis combustion energy of octane versus dihydrogen is incorrect.
